description: This plant was at the edge of the woods in partial sun. The top three suggestions are American bittersweet (Celastrus scandens), Oriental bittersweet (Celastrus orbiculatus), and possumhaw (Ilex decidua). American bittersweet is found in Massachusetts and all New England states. It has the same yellow/orange fruit and simple, alternate, serrated leaves. However, the leaves of this plant might be wider than the leaves of American bittersweet and have finer teeth on the margin. Fruits of American bittersweet are arranged in terminal panicles, while the fruits of Oriental bittersweet, and this plant, are found along the length of the stem at leaf axils. Oriental bittersweet also has a more similar leaf morphology to this plant, because the leaves are wider than American bittersweet with deeper teeth on the margins, and the leaves of American bittersweet have longer points. Leaf morphology is not as reliable for distinguishing between  American bittersweet and Oriental bittersweet as the position of the fruits. Possumhaw always has red fruits, not yellow/orange fruits, not yellow/orange. It does not seem common in New England, and is found in the Southeast part of the US.

description:
A few days ago, on a hike, I found a vine unknown to me, photographed it, and learned that it was in fact *Celastris scandens*, a species endangered in North Carolina. And to think I had at first disregarded the plant as probably not significant, but had sense enough to argue with myself that I had better go back and give it some respect wit the chance for me to learn something. *And I did!*

SO, imagine my surprise this morning whilst out watering plants in my mother-in-law's garden, that one of the large pots left by the previous owners, and in which was growing a culinary sage bush, there was also a *Celastris scandens*. It is almost unbelievable. I reckon a bird planted it there via its droppings. I consider it a serendipitous series of events of sheer delight.

I provided the plant a small trellis, just like the pot, a vestige of the previous owners' gardening exploits, found abandoned between a Rhododendron and the house foundation. It is curious how such unrelated things culminate in something so wonderful.

description:
Vouchered. Pics 8-10 showing frugivory maybe. Robins, flickers, cedar waxwings, finches, jays, chickadees all in immediate area. One study conducted on frugivory (fruit-eating) demonstrated round leaf bittersweet seed remaining in the gut of birds for 14-42 days (showing potential for long distance dispersal):
https://mnfi.anr.msu.edu/invasive-species/OrientalBittersweetBCP.pdf
This was a single individual and the only plant producing fruit in the population and it (as well as all fruit) was collected for vouchering and/or disposed of.

Pic 28 demonstrating leaf variability: shape ranging from suborbicular, obovate, ovate, to almost elliptic. Leaf tips range from obtuse to acuminate, though sometimes cuspidate. Leaf bases acute (cuneate) where meeting petiole. Fruits/inflorescences axillary.

Petiole length 7-27mm

Margins dentate & gland-tipped

Pics 35-37 abaxial veins minutely puberulent (10x)

11 fruits of varying size checked for viable seeds. ALL contained at least one viable seed. 15 viable seeds in total (vouchered) and 3 non-viable. Studies demonstrate 85%-95% germination in lab settings and similar germination in the field after a cold period.

@samleininger
